newsitem.title: USA: Cuomo gets earful at housing secretary hearing.
newsitem.headline: Cuomo gets earful at housing secretary hearing.

text.p: Housing Secretary nominee Andrew Cuomo was given an earful Wednesday about problems at the agency and said he would make improving management a top priority if confirmed.
Cuomo, an assistant secretary at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), was grilled by members of the Senate Banking Committee at a three-hour hearing on his nomination.
HUD has been under fire in Congress, accused of being inefficient, unwieldy and too costly.

Sen. Lauch Faircloth, a North Carolina Republican, who in the past introduced legislation to abolish HUD, said the agency had become a "massive" bureaucracy that had lost the ability to manage itself.

Cuomo, 39, said he was committed to reducing the number of HUD personnel by the year 2000 to 7,500 from 10,400 currently. He said he was also committed to improving management and financial accountability of the agency.
"It will be my top priority, period," Cuomo told senators.
Cuomo, son of former New York Gov. Mario Cuomo, was flanked at the hearing by his mother Matilda Cuomo and mother-in-law Ethel Kennedy. Cuomo's father was traveling and did not attend.

The nominee's wife, Kerry Kennedy Cuomo, and one of their two-year-old twin daughters, Cara, also attended the hearing which took on the air of a celebrity event. Even "Vanity Fair" magazine sent a reporter.
Cuomo was expected to be confirmed by the Senate to replace Henry Cisneros, who decided to leave the Cabinet mainly for financial reasons.

The Senate Banking Committee will vote on the nomination next Tuesday, committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato said, adding that he expected Cuomo to be approved. The nomination must then go before the full Senate.
"Assuming favorably, and I would think probably unanimous committee action," D'Amato said he hoped a vote before the full Senate would be scheduled next week.

The main concerns expressed by senators were that HUD was too big and unwieldy to operate efficiently and that "Section 8" government subsidized housing program for low-income people could become too costly.
Many contracts that the government has with property owners of Section 8 housing are expiring over the next few years and the renewal of those contracts will cost the government.

D'Amato displayed a chart at the hearing that showed assistance for the renewal of expiring Section 8 contracts would jump to $10.2 billion in fiscal 1998, which starts in October, from $3.6 billion in fiscal 1997. HUD's whole budget for fiscal 1997 was $19.5 billion.
"HUD faces a fiscal crisis. Hard choices must be made regarding discretionary spending priorities," said D'Amato, who supported Cuomo's nomination.
